title: Start Here: What You'll Learn and Why
summary: See what this course covers and in what order, why APIs and servers matter when you build for the web, and what you'll build with Spring Boot.
intro: In the web course, your pages asked servers for data with fetch, and JSON came back. This course teaches the other side: the code that answers. You'll build an API with Spring Boot, the framework most Java teams use for servers, from the first request it answers to a system that runs on many servers at once. This first lesson is the map: why a web developer needs to know how APIs and servers work, what Spring Boot is good at, what the course covers and in what order, what you'll build, and what you'll be able to do at the end. It assumes the web course and Learn Java, and nothing more.

steps.title: What a backend does, and why learn it
steps.body:
Before you spend a whole course on the server's side, it's worth knowing what a server does that a page can't do for itself, and why that matters even if you mostly build pages.

## What the backend does

Recall from the web course that a site has two halves. The **frontend** is the code that runs in the browser. The **backend** is the code that runs on a server, a computer somewhere else that answers requests. The two only ever talk through requests and responses.

A page can do a lot by itself, but some jobs need a backend:

- **Keeping data that outlasts the tab.** A room booked on a laptop has to show up on a phone tomorrow, and on everyone else's screen too. A browser's storage belongs to one browser on one device, so shared data lives on the server, in a **database**: a program built to store data safely and find it again fast.
- **Enforcing the rules.** Anyone can send any request, as curl showed in the web course, with no page involved at all. So a rule like one booking per room at a time can't live in the page's JavaScript, where it's easy to skip. The server checks every request, whoever sent it.
- **Keeping secrets.** Anything sent to a browser can be read by the person using it. Passwords, the key that charges a card, and the address of the database stay on the server.
- **Serving every kind of client.** The same data feeds a website, a phone app, and other companies' programs, and they all ask the same backend.

A backend offers those jobs through an **API**, which the web course described as addresses meant for programs rather than people, answering with data instead of pages. The next lesson defines it properly.

## Why learn it if you build pages

- **Every page you build talks to one.** When a fetch fails, the reason is in the response: its status code, its headers, its error message. Knowing how the server produced them turns guessing into reading.
- **The two halves meet in the middle.** Most teams expect web developers to change both sides, or at least to design the requests together. **Full-stack developer**, someone who works on both halves, is one of the most common web jobs.
- **Speed and safety live there too.** A slow page is often waiting on a slow API. Many of the data leaks in the news came through an API that answered requests it should have refused.
- **You can build the whole thing.** With a backend of your own, an idea for an app doesn't stop at a page that can't save anything.

## Spring Boot

**Spring Boot** is the **framework** most Java teams use for servers, code that calls yours, as the web course put it: it reads each request, hands it to the method you wrote for that address, and sends your answer back. It's the quick way to start an application on the **Spring Framework**, which has been around for more than twenty years, with a large family of projects around it for security, data, messaging, and batch jobs. Banks, insurers, airlines, and big shops run their core systems on it, and Netflix builds its Java services with it.

Spring Boot is good at:

- **Large business systems** that many developers work on for years. Java's types and tools catch mistakes early, and Spring's habits make one project look like the next.
- **Having a tested answer for almost everything**: security, databases, messaging, and monitoring.
- **Handling many requests at once**, each on its own **thread**, a line of work that runs alongside the others. A later lesson, Your First Spring Boot Project, shows how, including Java's newer virtual threads.

It uses more memory and starts slower than Node.js or Go. And much of its work happens through **annotations**, the `@` labels on classes and methods, like `@Override`, which can feel like magic until you know what each one does. This course shows you, one annotation at a time.

The two examples below show a whole small server and what it answers. You don't need to follow the code yet. By the end of the course, you'll write code like it without a second thought.

examples.title: A small Spring Boot controller
examples.prompt: A controller in `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/rooms/RoomController.java` that answers requests for Roombook's study rooms. Roombook is the API you'll build in this course.
examples.explanation: `@RestController` tells Spring that this class answers HTTP requests, and that what its methods return goes back as JSON. `@RequestMapping("/v1/rooms")` puts every method under that path. `Room` is a record, the short way to write a class that only holds data, and the map holds three rooms in memory for now. A later section moves them into a database. `@GetMapping("/{roomId}")` says: when a GET request arrives for a path like `/v1/rooms/1`, call this method, and `@PathVariable` turns that spot of the path into a `long`. `ResponseEntity` is the whole response: `notFound()` answers 404, and `ok(room)` answers 200 with the room. A small class with a `main` method, which every new project comes with, starts it all. Notice what you didn't write: nothing reads bytes, writes headers, or turns the record into JSON. Spring does that, and calls your method in between.

examples.title: What a client sees
examples.prompt: With the server running, ask it for room 1 from a terminal. As in the web course, `-i` tells curl to show the status line and the headers, not only the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:06:09 GMT

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
examples.explanation: The status line says `200` with no words after it. Tomcat, the server program inside Spring Boot, leaves them out, since only the number counts. `Content-Type: application/json` says the body is JSON: Spring turned the record into JSON with a library called Jackson. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` means the body is sent in pieces, each with its own length, in place of a `Content-Length` header up front. The body is the room as one line of JSON: the same data as the record, now text that any program in any language can read. Ask for room 99 and this small version answers a `404` with no body at all, from `notFound()`. From the lesson on routes on, Roombook's 404s carry a JSON body that says what went wrong.

steps.title: The path through the course
steps.body:
Knowing where you're headed makes each lesson easier to place. When you learn to read a request's body, it helps to know you'll soon check every field in it. When you store bookings in a database, it helps to know that two people will try to book the same room in the same second. So here's the whole path, in order.

```diagram start-here-course-path
Each section builds on the ones before it, so take them in order.
```

It runs in three stretches. First you learn what APIs and servers are, and start a project. Then you build the API one layer at a time, from its first routes to a tested service. Last, you run it on many servers and get it ready for real traffic. Beside each section, the diagram shows what Roombook, the course's API, gains in it. The last part of this lesson describes Roombook.

## 1. APIs and Servers

What an API is, who calls one and why, and what a server really is. Then the styles APIs come in, like REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, and webhooks, and when each one fits. Last, you install Spring Boot, create the project, and answer your first request. Along the way you'll see how the JVM, the program that runs Java, serves many requests at once on many threads, which explains most of what makes a Spring Boot server fast or slow.

## 2. Handling Requests

The everyday work of an API. You'll connect each method and path to the code that handles it, answer with the right status code, and read every part of a request: the path, the query string, the headers, and a JSON body. Then **middleware**, code that runs before and after every request for jobs like logging, and how to check every input and answer every error in one format. In Spring Boot, middleware comes in a few kinds, called filters, interceptors, and controller advice, and annotations from Bean Validation, Java's standard for checking data, check the input.

## 3. Structure and Data

How to split an API's code into layers, so each part has one job. Spring's container, which creates your objects and hands each one what it needs, wires the layers together. Then databases: why an API needs one, how SQL and NoSQL databases differ, and how to turn Roombook's rules into tables. You'll write SQL by hand for **PostgreSQL**, a popular SQL database, using Spring's JdbcClient, and keep the data correct with constraints and transactions, so two people can never book the same room at once. Room feedback goes in **MongoDB**, a NoSQL database.

## 4. Authentication and Authorization

**Authentication** is finding out who's calling, and **authorization** is deciding what they may do. You'll store passwords safely, log people in with sessions and cookies, issue tokens to phone apps, give machines API keys, let staff sign in with their university account, and check on every request that the caller may touch what they ask for. Spring Security, a chain of checks that runs in front of your controllers, does much of the work.

## 5. Using and Testing the API

The API from the caller's side: calling it with curl and Postman, describing every endpoint in an OpenAPI document that tools turn into docs and client code, and changing it without breaking anyone. Then tests that prove each piece works, from one function to the whole running API. A library called springdoc writes the OpenAPI document from your controllers, and you'll test with JUnit, AssertJ, and MockMvcTester, the testing tools most Spring teams use.

## 6. Distributed Systems

What changes when one server isn't enough: running many copies behind a **load balancer**, a server that spreads requests across them, and sharing what they need in **Redis**, a very fast store kept in memory, for caching, sessions, rate limits, and live updates. Then surviving slow or failing services with timeouts, retries, and keys that make a request safe to send twice, plus health checks and shutting down without dropping a request. Last, databases at scale: copies of the database that share the reading, and data split across many databases. These ideas run every large site, and they come up in job interviews too.

## 7. Production

Getting it ready for real users: the attacks APIs face most and how to stop them, packing the API into a **Docker** image that runs the same on any computer, releasing new versions safely, and seeing inside it while it runs, with logs, metrics, and traces.

## After this course

The React and Next.js courses build the other half: web apps that call APIs like Roombook. And every backend stack faces the same problems you'll solve here, so the ideas carry over to whichever one your next job uses.

steps.title: What you'll build and how you'll work
steps.body:
A course reads better with something real at the end of it. Here's what you'll build, how you'll work on it, and what you'll be able to do once you're done.

## Roombook, a study-room booking API

The examples all come from one API: **Roombook**, which lets students book group study rooms in a university's libraries. The campus has two buildings, the Main Library and the Science Library, with rooms like Turing, which seats 6, Lovelace, which seats 4, and Hopper, which seats 8.

It has real rules, the kind that make backend work interesting:

- A booking starts and ends on the hour or the half hour, and lasts from 30 minutes to 3 hours, inside the building's opening hours.
- It starts in the future, at most 14 days ahead, and it fits the room: no more people than seats.
- A student holds at most 3 upcoming bookings at a time.
- Two bookings for the same room never overlap, even when two people press Book in the same second.
- Students can cancel their own bookings, and library staff can cancel any booking in their building.

It has real callers too: the Roombook website, a phone app, small screens by each room's door that show the day's schedule, and library staff who sign in with their university account. Each one proves who it is in a different way, which is what the Authentication and Authorization section is about.

Lesson by lesson, Roombook gains:

- endpoints for buildings, rooms, and bookings, with every input checked
- PostgreSQL tables, and constraints that make a double booking impossible
- room feedback, stored in MongoDB
- sign-up and login, tokens for the phone app, keys for the door screens, and university sign-in for staff
- an OpenAPI document, and tests at every level
- a Redis cache, rate limits, a live stream of room availability, and webhooks that tell other apps about bookings
- a Docker image, with logs, metrics, and traces to watch it run

## Where you'll work

In the Playground, the same folder on your own computer as in the web course, with the Explorer, the editor, and the terminal. Roombook runs in the Playground's terminal at `http://localhost:8080`, and you'll send it requests from a second terminal, your computer's own, with curl, the way the web course did. Later you'll add **Postman**, an app for sending requests and saving them to send again. Most lessons don't need a browser at all, since an API's clients are programs. The database lessons show how to run PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis on your computer too.

## How the lessons work

The same way as in the web course. Each lesson is split into parts, each part opens on why its idea matters, and every new word is explained the first time it appears. Code is for reading and copying, and you try it in the Playground. Output is always real, copied from an actual run, so the times, ids, and version numbers in yours will differ.

The code is Java 25 with Spring Boot 4.2, built with Maven through the `./mvnw` script that every project carries. If yours are newer, the code still works, and only the version numbers in the output change.

## What you'll be able to do

By the end of the course, you'll be able to:

- Explain what an API and a server are, and pick the right API style for a job.
- Build a REST API with Spring Boot that checks every input and answers every error in one standard format.
- Store data in PostgreSQL with SQL you write yourself, and in MongoDB, and keep it correct when requests race.
- Log people in safely with sessions, tokens, API keys, and single sign-on, and check permissions on every request.
- Document the API with OpenAPI, and test it at every level.
- Run it on many servers with Redis, timeouts, retries, and database replicas.
- Defend it against the most common attacks, ship it in Docker, and watch it with logs, metrics, and traces.

The next lesson starts with the word this whole course is about: API.

recap:
- A backend keeps shared data, enforces the rules, keeps secrets, and serves every kind of client through an API.
- Knowing how servers work helps you read a failed request, design requests with your team, and build whole apps.
- Spring Boot is the framework most Java teams use, strong at large business systems, with a tested answer for almost everything.
- The course goes in order: APIs and servers, handling requests, structure and data, auth, using and testing, distributed systems, then production.
- You'll build Roombook, a study-room booking API with real rules and four kinds of callers.
- You'll run it in the Playground and call it with curl, and every output shown is real.
